name: Llano del Rio
ideal: Job Harriman's socialist cooperative colony; Alice Constance Austin's circular city with kitchenless houses, central kitchens and communal childcare to free women from domestic labour.
reality: Austin's city was never built — colonists lived in tents and adobe shacks around a hotel, dairy and laundry. Big Rock Creek water proved unreliable and the state refused a dam permit. Peak ~1,100 members (1917); abandoned 1918; ~60 families moved to New Llano, Louisiana. Stone ruins remain: California Historical Landmark No. 933.

name: Little Landers (Los Terrenitos), Tujunga
ideal: William E. Smythe's agrarian colony: 'a little land and a living' — family subsistence plots and cooperative self-government.
reality: Rocky soil defeated the plots; Little Landers, Inc. was dissolved in 1917 for unpaid taxes and lots were subdivided and resold — by 1925 almost all original settlers had left. Only the 1913 clubhouse survives: Bolton Hall, Historic-Cultural Monument No. 2, now a museum.
geomnote: Bolton Hall, LA Historic-Cultural Monument No. 2 (City parcel boundary)

name: Baldwin Hills Village (Village Green)
ideal: Clarence Stein's fullest version of the Radburn / Garden City idea: a car-free superblock of 627 rental homes facing shared greens, garages pushed to the edge.
reality: Built and still intact — but converted to condominiums. National Historic Landmark (2001). The superblock was never repeated at scale; the city around it was platted as conventional lots.
geomnote: Village Green, LA Historic-Cultural Monument No. 174 (City boundary); National Historic Landmark

name: Crestwood Hills (Mutual Housing Association)
ideal: A cooperative founded by four musicians that grew to ~400 member families: modernist houses by A. Quincy Jones and Whitney R. Smith, a shared nursery school, park and community centre on a Brentwood hillside.
reality: To obtain mortgage financing the co-op had to accept racial covenants — its one minority couple was asked to withdraw. The 1961 Bel Air–Brentwood fire destroyed 49 homes. The cooperative dissolved into ordinary ownership; the park and co-op preschool survive.
geomnote: Mutual Housing Association Site Office, LA Historic-Cultural Monument No. 680, 990 Hanley Ave

name: Elysian Park Heights → Dodger Stadium
ideal: Richard Neutra and Robert Alexander's public-housing city for Chavez Ravine: ~3,400–3,600 homes in 24 thirteen-storey towers and 163 low-rises, with schools and shared grounds.
reality: The Mexican-American communities of La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop were cleared for it, then the project was cancelled in 1953 amid red-scare attacks on public housing. The land went to the Dodgers (1958); the last holdouts were evicted in May 1959; Dodger Stadium opened 10 April 1962.
geomnote: Dodger Stadium site: Assessor parcels 5415-018-010/-015/-016 (2025 roll)
